name: Domaine du Pégau Châteauneuf-du-Pape Cuvée Réservée 2010
text:
## Domaine du Pégau Châteauneuf-du-Pape Cuvée Réservée 2010

**The story.** Domaine du Pégau is one of the great traditional names of [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC). The Féraud family can trace its roots in the village to the middle of the 17th century, when its ancestors planted vines among their olive and fruit trees. Laurence Féraud's great-grandparents brought the family into the wine business; their vines were later divided among four children. Her father, Paul Féraud, began bottling his own wine from a 5-hectare parcel he inherited; before that the grapes were sold to merchants. Laurence joined him in 1987, when the family had 7 hectares, and has run the estate since the 2005 vintage ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

The wine was once bottled as Domaine Féraud. The family renamed it Pégau after an old Provençal word for a wine jug: the "pégau" is an ancient jug found during 14th-century excavations at the popes' palace in Avignon, the [Palais des Papes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_Papes) ([see it from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k)). Even the family can't agree on how to say it: Laurence says "Pay-Go", her father "Puh-Gow" ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The vineyards.** Pégau has 21 hectares in Châteauneuf, in 11 parcels, on stones, clay and [limestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limestone). The best vines are on the plateau of [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k), with its big rounded stones, the [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), and the oldest were planted in 1902. In 2012 the family added about 60 hectares in the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC), near [Sorgues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorgues), as Château Pégau ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The wine: Cuvée Réservée.** This is Pégau's classic, a benchmark of old-school Châteauneuf. It is mostly [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), with [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah), [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre), [Counoise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counoise) and other varieties. The grapes are not destemmed; the whole bunches ferment with wild yeasts in traditional cement vats, and the wine then ages about two years in old foudres of many origins, the oldest nearly 90 years old and made from Russian oak. About 6,500 cases are made ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). For 2010, Robert Parker gave the blend as 80% Grenache, 12% Syrah, 4% Mourvèdre and 4% other varieties, at 14.8% alcohol, slightly lower than the 2009 ([Farr Vintners, critics' notes](https://www.farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=31576)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) calls 2010 "a very successful vintage" in the southern Rhône, with precision and freshness letting the terroir show, outstanding for both reds and whites. She adds that the wines perhaps haven't matured quite as spectacularly as first expected. At Pégau, Paul Féraud preferred the 2009 and Laurence the 2010, and Parker called it a "pick'em" dilemma between the two.

**What the critics say for 2010.** As listed by [Farr Vintners](https://www.farrvintners.com/wine.php?wine=31576) and [Benchmark Wine](https://www.benchmarkwine.com/products/12306-pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-cuvee-reservee-2010):
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck), Wine Advocate: 98** (October 2013). "A brilliant vintage for Laurence": classic Pégau ripe dark fruit, [garrigue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrigue), cured meats, tobacco leaf, saddle leather and a hint of game; full-bodied and concentrated, with thrilling depth and a blockbuster finish. Quite polished for this estate, yet it "screams southern France". Drink 2016 to 2030, and it will thrill for two to three decades.
- **[Robert Parker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Parker_%28wine_critic%29), Wine Advocate: 96 to 98+** (from foudre, October 2012). Exceptional intensity and full-bodied power, a little more reserved than the flamboyant 2009, with Provençal herbs, smoke, meat, [kirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirsch), blackcurrant and blackberry. He expected it to age for three decades or more, judging by how well the 1989 and 1990 were maturing.
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 97** (James Molesworth, August 2013). Intense, with the tarry, bittersweet cocoa grip of the vintage, crushed plum, blackberry and braised fig, and a muscular finish of brick dust, pepper and smouldering charcoal. "A throwback profile... and it works." Best 2015 to 2035; 6,580 cases made.
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 97** (from the vintage list on his producer page). He says the Réservée is his personal favourite of Pégau's wines.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.8** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is sixteen years old. Dunnuck's window runs to 2030, Wine Spectator's to 2035, and Parker expected three decades or more. The Wine Cellar Insider says Pégau drinks best from 7 to 25 years after the vintage. So it is in its prime now: expect the fruit to have softened into leather, game, dried herbs and earth, the classic "old Pégau" style. Decant gently, mainly to leave the sediment behind, and drink it over the next several years.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, and only enough [decanting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) for older vintages to leave the sediment behind ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). Pégau is famous for a wild, gamy side, so let it breathe in the glass and watch it change over the evening.

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, grilled meats, sausages, barbecue and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus mushrooms and cheese. With a mature, gamy Pégau, my picks are roast [venison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venison) or game birds, a beef [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube), [wild boar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_boar) stew, or a mushroom dish with [truffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuber_melanosporum). I'd avoid delicate fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Pégau 2010. It turns up with back-vintage merchants such as [Benchmark Wine](https://www.benchmarkwine.com/products/12306-pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-cuvee-reservee-2010) and at auction. A sixteen-year-old Pégau from a great vintage is a treat to own.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V), a former Archbishop of Bordeaux, moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name, "the Pope's new castle". The wine became known as "Vin du Pape" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Phylloxera.** The [phylloxera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_French_Wine_Blight) louse reached Châteauneuf in the early 1870s, earlier than most French regions, and wiped out the vineyards. Before the First World War, much of the replanted wine was sold to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) as "vin de médecine" to strengthen thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law on 15 May 1936. One of the baron's rules: vines could only be planted on land dry enough to grow both [lavender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavandula) and [thyme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thyme) ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **A jug from the popes' palace.** The estate's name honours the "pégau", a wine jug discovered during 14th-century excavations at the Palais des Papes in Avignon, the palace built during the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy) ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Curious details**
- **Da Capo.** Pégau's ultra-rare Cuvée da Capo is made only in the very best years (so far 1998, 2000, 2003, 2007 and 2010), and Jeff Leve gave the 2010 da Capo 100 points ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/pegau-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)). Your Réservée comes from the same great year.
- **Wines for the children.** Two one-off cuvées were made in honour of the family's children: Cuvée Maxime 1995 and Cuvée Justine 1997, about 100 cases each.
- **Music in the bottle.** The back label of Pégau's white Cuvée A Tempo has a code that, scanned with a phone, plays a piece of music written for the wine.
- **One wine, many bottlings.** Older Pégau vintages (1990 and earlier) were sometimes bottled on three dates almost a year apart, so bottles of the same vintage can differ; today the bottling is standardised.
- **The famous stones.** Much of Châteauneuf is covered in [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), smooth [quartzite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartz) stones left by Alpine glaciers and rounded over millennia by the [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne). They soak up the sun by day and give the heat back to the vines at night, and in dry summers they help keep moisture in the soil ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force, and a Californian Rhône-style wine from [Bonny Doon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonny_Doon_Vineyard), Le Cigare Volant, is named after the tale ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and most wines come in at 14 to 15.5%. Yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare, nearly half what [Bordeaux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine) allows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
